description.value: The study examined whether neural responses to high-calorie food pictures before and after a 12-week psychosocial weight-loss program predicted short-term weight loss and 9-month weight maintenance in obese participants.

design.value: A longitudinal design was used in which obese participants were scanned before and after a 12-wk behavioral, psychosocial weight-loss program, with a 9-mo follow-up weight measurement. Normal-weight controls were also imaged twice, 12 wk apart, but did not participate in the EatRight program.

description.value: 25 obese (n = 21) and overweight (n = 4) adults enrolled in the 12-wk EatRight Lifestyle Weight Management Program; for brevity, the authors refer to this group as obese.

inclusion_criteria.value: BMI ≥ 25 and participation in the EatRight Lifestyle Weight Management Program

recruitment_method.value: Obese participants were recruited at one of the first three (of 12) EatRight classes.

medical_condition.value: Type II diabetes in two participants
depression treated with antidepressants in three participants

clinical_characteristics.value: Initial BMI range was 28.4 to 44.6 kg/m2, with mean ± SD 32.86 ± 3.82. Participants attended a 12-wk psychosocial weight-loss program. In the obese group, 88% lost weight, 8% remained stable, and 4% gained weight during treatment. At 9-mo follow-up, mean weight change was +0.75 ± 5.02%, with 17% approximately stable, 38% losing additional weight, and 46% gaining weight.

medication_status.value: Two obese participants were on metformin, glipizide, and/or lantus to manage Type II diabetes. Three obese participants were being treated with a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and had been on medication for more than 6 months without changing medication between scanning sessions.

description.value: Normal-weight controls recruited from UAB and the surrounding community; they were imaged twice, 12 wk apart, but did not participate in the EatRight program.

exclusion_criteria.value: The same handedness, cognitive, medical, psychiatric, substance-use, MRI-safety, vision, blood-pressure, eating-disorder, dietary, immigration, and other criteria applied to the participants.

recruitment_method.value: Recruited from UAB and the surrounding community using flyers and advertisements posted in the UAB Reporter newspaper.

clinical_characteristics.value: BMI < 25. There was no significant change in body weight from Session 1 to Session 2.

task_name.value: viewing high-calorie food vs. control pictures

task_description.value: Participants viewed high-calorie sweet food, high-calorie savory food, low-calorie food, and car pictures during six 3:15 min fMRI runs at each of two scanning sessions. Each run consisted of two pseudorandomly presented epochs each of car and low-calorie food images, and one epoch each of high-calorie sweet food and high-calorie savory food images.

instructions.value: Participants were instructed to eat a normal breakfast and then refrain from eating for 8 h before being imaged, abstain from alcohol for 24 h, avoid exercise on the day of the study, and avoid caffeine for 3 h prior to imaging.

stimuli.value: 504 high-quality color photographs: 168 food images and 84 control images for each session. The food images included 84 high-calorie foods, equally divided between sweet and savory foods, and 84 low-calorie foods. Control images depicted cars. No image was shown more than once.

task_performance_measures.value: Percentage of pictures correctly identified as having been seen during each fMRI scan.

instrument.value: Philips Achieva 3 T ultra-short (1.57 m) bore magnet, housed in UAB's Cardiovascular MRI facility

description.value: Functional MR images were acquired using single-shot gradient echo T2*-weighted echo-planar imaging (EPI) with blood oxygenation level dependent (BOLD) contrast. Six runs were collected at each of the pre- and post-treatment scanning sessions. Each run consisted of 65 volumes. The first 2 scans were discarded to allow for the BOLD signal to stabilize. Half of the participants were imaged using a 6-channel head coil and half using an 8-channel head coil; the same head coil was used for both sessions for each participant.

pulse_sequence_type.value: single-shot gradient echo T2*-weighted echo-planar imaging (EPI)

instrument.value: Philips Achieva 3 T ultra-short (1.57 m) bore magnet, housed in UAB's Cardiovascular MRI facility

description.value: High-resolution T1-weighted scans were acquired using a 160-slice 3D T1 Turbo-field Echo (TFE) volume sequence and were used to exclude participants with gross brain abnormality.

Functional images were slice time-corrected, spatially realigned, normalized to standard Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) brain space, spatially smoothed, high-pass filtered, and temporally filtered using an autoregressive model.

steps.value: Functional images were slice time-corrected to the onset of the 15th slice (middle slice).
Spatial realignment was performed using INRIAlign, a motion correction algorithm unbiased by local signal changes.
During realignment, a mean functional image was computed for each run and matched to the EPI template provided within SPM8.
Data were spatially normalized to standard Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) brain space.
Data were spatially smoothed using a three-dimensional Gaussian kernel of 6 mm full-width at half-maximum (FWHM), resulting in a resampled in-plane resolution of 2 × 2 × 2 mm voxels.
The functional data were passed through a 1/128 Hz high-pass filter to remove low-frequency artifacts.
The functional data were temporally filtered using an autoregressive (AR(1)) model.
No participant's data set failed the movement inclusionary criteria of no more than 2 mm translational movement and 2° rotational movement within a run before correction.

model_settings.value: Single-subject contrast maps were generated voxel by voxel. Separate regressors were created for high-calorie food, low-calorie food, and car images by convolving the time course of activation, using a boxcar function, with the canonical HRF. Fixed-effects analyses were performed for each individual participant for both imaging sessions, examining high-calorie foods versus cars and high-calorie foods versus low-calorie foods.

Second-level group analyses were performed using a random-effects model of the beta images from the single-subject contrast maps. Multiple regressions related activation for the high-calorie foods versus cars contrast to percent weight change, with initial BMI as a covariate; weight change during the program was added as an additional covariate in the two analyses of 9-mo weight change.
